title: Proxima Bank - escalation check-in (capacity protection / 429s)
summary: Follow-up after Proxima’s Jan escalation tied to burst traffic on /v1/chat/completions. Redwood reviewed the new hot-route capacity protection behavior (tier-aware admission control + consistent 429 reason codes). Proxima confirmed stability improved (lower tail latency, fewer 5xx) but noted increased 429s during morning batch + interactive overlap. Teams aligned on which 429s are expected vs actionable, and on an exception process for temporary burst increases (with guardrails and advance notice).
topics: Recap of escalation: tail latency + intermittent 5xx during peak
Post-change results: p95/p99 latency and error rates
429 reason codes: quota vs overload/admission control
Client retry/backoff guidance and streaming behavior expectations
Exception handling: temporary burst allowances and change management
Next steps: dashboards, threshold review, follow-up cadence
next_steps: Redwood to send a one-pager mapping 429 reason codes to recommended client behavior (retry vs don’t retry) and the escalation path.
Proxima to share their current concurrency caps and retry policy configuration for interactive vs batch traffic (especially the 8:30–10:00 UTC overlap window).
Redwood to evaluate a temporary +20% burst allowance on the protected chat route in eu-west with explicit guardrails (timeboxed, monitored) and confirm by EOW.
Schedule a 45-min technical session with Proxima engineering to review their request shaping (max_tokens, prompt lengths) and how it impacts admission thresholds.
action_items: Rachel Kim: Email recap + links to dashboards and the support article on 429 reason codes by 2026-01-16.
Rafael Mendes: Pull last 14 days of Proxima tiered metrics (429 by reason, p95/p99 latency, shed rate) for eu-west and us-east and share screenshots by 2026-01-16.
Liam O'Rourke: Draft exception request (temporary burst increase) with start/end date, max RPS/concurrency, and rollback criteria for Proxima approval by 2026-01-17.
Anika Rao: Provide Proxima’s retry/backoff settings and whether they treat all 429s uniformly by 2026-01-17.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Proxima Bank - escalation check-in (capacity protection / 429s)
Date: 2026-01-15
Start time: 17:03 UTC
Duration: 34 min

Attendees:
- Rachel Kim (Redwood Inference)
- Liam O'Rourke (Redwood Inference)
- Rafael Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Owen Phillips (Redwood Inference)
- Anika Rao (Proxima Bank)
- Martin Schulte (Proxima Bank)
- Jules Bennett (Proxima Bank)
- Sana Qureshi (Proxima Bank)

Auto-summary (generated):
- Proxima reported fewer timeouts and improved tail latency since Redwood enabled enterprise route protection.
- Increased 429s observed during overlap of batch summarization jobs and interactive advisor traffic.
- Redwood clarified 429 reason codes and which are retriable.
- Agreed on process for temporary burst exceptions with monitoring + rollback.


00:00 Rachel Kim: Hey everyone. Thanks for making time. The goal today is just to close the loop on last week’s escalation and make sure the behavior you’re seeing now matches expectations, and then align on the exception process so we’re not doing this ad hoc at 2 a.m.

00:15 Anika Rao: Sounds good. Appreciate you all jumping on. We’ve got Sana from vendor, Martin from SRE, Jules from the team that owns the gateway.

00:24 Liam O'Rourke: Great, thanks. I’m Liam, your TAM. Rafael is SRE lead on our side, and Owen helped coordinate the support escalation.

00:34 Owen Phillips: Hi.

00:36 Rachel Kim: Before we dive into metrics, Anika, do you want to recap in your words what went wrong and what “good” looks like for you? Just to make sure we’re aligned.

00:46 Anika Rao: Yeah. So the incident was essentially Monday/Tuesday our morning peak—like 8:30 to 10:00 UTC—we saw a bunch of end-user requests timing out. It wasn’t all of them but enough to trigger our internal alerting. And we saw some 5xx from Redwood. We also saw higher latency p99 like, I don’t know, 18 seconds which for our advisor workflow is basically unusable.

01:08 Anika Rao: “Good” looks like: the interactive advisor chat should remain stable, even if our batch summarization jobs have to slow down. And we want something deterministic. Like, if we’re going to get throttled, we want a clear signal and we can backoff.

01:25 Rachel Kim: Yep. That matches exactly why we did the capacity protection rollout. Rafael, do you want to share what we’re seeing since enabling it for Proxima’s enterprise routes?

01:34 Rafael Mendes: Sure. And I’ll caveat: I’m looking at our internal dashboards, not your side, so we should compare with what Martin is seeing. But for eu-west—where most of your traffic is landing—starting Jan 8 we enabled protected route policy for your enterprise tier on /v1/chat/completions and embeddings.

01:54 Rafael Mendes: Since then, p95 on chat has been steady around 1.6 to 2.1 seconds. p99 is mostly under 4.5 seconds. There are spikes, but the big difference is we’re not seeing the long tail runs where queue depth goes unbounded and then everything melts.

02:14 Martin Schulte: That aligns. I mean our client-side shows improvement. We used to see these long “hockey sticks” in latency graphs. Now we get more 429s but the successful requests come back faster.

02:26 Jules Bennett: Yeah, agreed. It feels like you’re pushing back instead of letting it time out.

02:32 Rachel Kim: That’s exactly it. The system is choosing to shed or throttle best-effort earlier to preserve the enterprise SLO. The tradeoff is you will see 429s if you exceed your configured budget during a pressure window.

02:47 Sana Qureshi: Sorry, can I ask a basic question—when you say “budget,” is that contractual? Or is that like a technical limit.

02:55 Rachel Kim: Good question. It’s a technical enforcement aligned to the tier semantics in your agreement. The contractual part is the SLO for the protected routes and how we prioritize enterprise traffic. The exact numbers—like burst allowance—are configurable within guardrails.

03:12 Liam O'Rourke: And we can do timeboxed exceptions if there’s a business need, but we want to avoid destabilizing the fleet.

03:19 Anika Rao: That brings me to the main thing. We’re happy with latency stability. The 429 volume, though, is higher than we expected. Martin, can you share what you pulled?

03:28 Martin Schulte: Yeah. Over the last week we’re seeing 429s peak at around 4–6% of requests during that overlap window. Outside that window it’s below 1%. We also noticed the reason code changes. Some say “quota” and some say “overload” or “admission.” The client treats them the same right now and retries, which might be part of the problem.

03:52 Rafael Mendes: Yep. That’s a key point. Not all 429s should be retried the same way.

03:58 Jules Bennett: Our current policy is basically exponential backoff with jitter and we retry up to, uh, five times. We didn’t differentiate.

04:07 Rachel Kim: Okay. Let’s break down the 429 types in plain language.

04:12 Owen Phillips: And just to note, the strings might differ a bit depending on which header your code is reading. We standardized recently, but I’ve seen folks parse the message body and that’s not stable.

04:22 Rachel Kim: Right. So: one bucket is “quota exceeded”—that typically means you’ve hit the per-minute or per-day allowance. Retrying immediately won’t help until the window resets.

04:35 Rachel Kim: The other bucket is “overload / admission control.” That means the system is under pressure and we’re intentionally gating lower priority traffic first. For enterprise protected routes, we try to preserve your latency SLO, but if your own traffic is above your enterprise budget, you can get 429 as well.

04:55 Rafael Mendes: And in that case, retries can work if you backoff appropriately and you reduce concurrency. If you retry aggressively at the same concurrency you just amplify the load and you’ll keep bouncing.

05:09 Martin Schulte: Is there a way to tell which is which reliably? We saw a header, I think “x-redwood-retry-after-ms” sometimes.

05:17 Owen Phillips: Yeah, that’s the right idea. There’s a Retry-After plus our own header. The key is the reason code header. Depending on your integration you should see something like “x-redwood-429-reason.” Sometimes it’s “quota_window” vs “overload_shed” vs “admission_control.”

05:34 Jules Bennett: I saw “shed” once, yeah.

05:37 Anika Rao: And “shed” means you dropped the request completely?

05:41 Rafael Mendes: Correct. It means we didn’t enqueue it to the GPU pool. We rejected early to avoid queue buildup. From a user perspective you get a fast 429 rather than a slow timeout.

05:52 Rachel Kim: The good news is: that’s the system working as designed to protect the rest of your traffic. The “bad” news is you need client logic to handle it cleanly.

06:05 Anika Rao: Understood. But we still need the batch jobs to complete. We can slow them, but they can’t just fail.

06:11 Liam O'Rourke: Totally. One pattern we recommend is separate concurrency pools: interactive has strict limits and higher priority, batch has a lower cap and uses the Retry-After signal. Or shift batch to a different route/model if that’s viable.

06:28 Jules Bennett: We could do that. Right now they share the same API key and same route.

06:34 Martin Schulte: We can split keys. But do you do priority per API key or per account tier?

06:40 Rafael Mendes: Primarily per tier and route group, and then per key can map to a class if you have multiple projects. Liam can confirm the exact setup on your account.

06:49 Liam O'Rourke: Yeah. For Proxima, you have one enterprise workspace today. We can create a second project for batch workloads that is best-effort within your org, if you want hard separation. That’s operationally simpler.

07:06 Anika Rao: That might be what we do. Sana will ask what that does to billing and reporting.

07:11 Sana Qureshi: Yes, we need cost allocation.

07:14 Liam O'Rourke: Reporting becomes better actually because you can tag usage per project. No pricing changes required. It’s more about quota enforcement and analytics.

07:24 Rachel Kim: Coming back to the 429s you’re seeing: Rafael, can you confirm whether those are mostly quota-window vs overload?

07:30 Rafael Mendes: For the overlap window in eu-west, it’s mostly admission-control overload, not daily quota. The quota-window ones are low. The admission control triggers correlate with queue depth crossing the threshold when you have long prompts.

07:47 Jules Bennett: Long prompts from the advisor context. We do retrieval plus a lot of prior conversation.

07:52 Rafael Mendes: Exactly. Sequence length matters. The scheduler has to allocate KV cache, and the long context requests can reduce throughput for the pool. That’s why you can hit admission even at the same request per second.

08:07 Martin Schulte: So if we cap max_tokens or shorten prompt, that helps.

08:11 Rafael Mendes: Yes. Shorter prompt and controlling max output tokens both reduce tail and reduce the chance you hit the queue depth threshold.

08:21 Anika Rao: That’s helpful but we also want to discuss whether we should get a higher burst budget. We have a predictable morning peak.

08:31 Rachel Kim: Yep, let’s talk exceptions. Our philosophy is: default budgets protect the fleet and your SLO. Exceptions are possible if we can bound the risk.

08:42 Owen Phillips: And we need a paper trail so support isn’t guessing what’s allowed when you page us.

08:48 Sana Qureshi: What’s the process exactly? Like do we email you, open a ticket, how long does it take.

08:55 Rachel Kim: We’ll formalize it, but today: you open a support ticket with “burst exception request,” include the route, region, expected RPS/concurrency, and the timeframe. Then Liam plus SRE review. If approved, we apply it behind a feature flag with rollback criteria.

09:15 Liam O'Rourke: And we typically timebox to 2–4 weeks, then revisit with real metrics.

09:22 Anika Rao: Okay. For us, the peak is daily, but it’s not a one-off. So we might need a permanent adjustment.

09:30 Rafael Mendes: Permanent is possible if we can validate capacity and if it doesn’t violate the protected route behavior. Another option is shifting some batch to off-peak or to a dedicated capacity block.

09:43 Anika Rao: We’re not ready for dedicated yet. Procurement-wise it’s a later conversation.

09:47 Liam O'Rourke: Understood. Let’s treat this as a temporary exception first to stabilize, then we can revisit dedicated if it becomes a recurring need.

09:57 Jules Bennett: Can we talk about what numbers you’re thinking? Like we need concrete.

10:03 Rafael Mendes: I don’t want to quote exact numbers on the call without double checking the policy config, but directionally: we can consider increasing burst by ~20% for your enterprise chat route in eu-west, with a hard cap on concurrency and with the requirement you implement differentiated retry.

10:23 Martin Schulte: That seems reasonable.

10:26 Anika Rao: What’s the risk from your side?

10:29 Rafael Mendes: The risk is if everyone gets an exception, the exception becomes the new normal and we’re back to queue blowups. For you specifically, risk is mostly correlated burst with long context length. If you spike and you retry aggressively, it still harms you and potentially others.

10:48 Rachel Kim: So our guardrails would be: we increase burst, but you cap batch concurrency and adopt Retry-After. And we monitor shed rate. If shed rate exceeds X for Y minutes, we roll back.

11:03 Jules Bennett: Makes sense.

11:05 Sana Qureshi: We’ll need that documented.

11:07 Rachel Kim: We’ll send a one-pager. Also, we can add you to incident-bot notifications for overload events on your account so you get proactive heads-up.

11:18 Martin Schulte: That would be great.

11:20 Liam O'Rourke: Quick check: are you seeing any weirdness with streaming? I know you had one complaint where the stream ended abruptly.

11:27 Jules Bennett: Actually yes, we saw a couple where the stream terminates and the client interprets it as success but the text is incomplete.

11:34 Owen Phillips: That’s a known edge case we fixed in late December for some clients, but depending on SDK version you might still see it. When shedding happens mid-stream, we send a consistent termination signal now. If you’re parsing the last chunk incorrectly, it can look like success.

11:51 Jules Bennett: We’re using our own SSE parser.

11:54 Owen Phillips: Okay. We can share the expected semantics and you can validate. But note: most shedding should happen before enqueue, so mid-stream should be rare.

12:06 Rafael Mendes: In the last week, I see almost all rejections are pre-admission. Mid-stream aborts are near zero for your account.

12:13 Martin Schulte: That matches. The incomplete streams were earlier.

12:17 Anika Rao: So the big thing for us is: we accept more 429s if it means lower tail. But we need to classify them and make sure batch can finish.

12:27 Rachel Kim: Exactly. Another point: do you want “priority” language in your internal messaging? We’ve found some banks prefer “capacity protection” language.

12:36 Sana Qureshi: Yes, please. “Priority” triggers procurement flags. Capacity protection sounds like resiliency.

12:43 Liam O'Rourke: Noted.

12:45 Rachel Kim: Martin, can you share what you’re doing today when you see 429? Do you surface it to end users?

12:52 Martin Schulte: For interactive we show a “please retry” banner, but it’s not great. We want to reduce user-facing errors.

13:00 Anika Rao: Ideally interactive doesn’t hit 429 at all, or very rarely.

13:05 Rafael Mendes: With the protection, interactive should be stable as long as it’s within the enterprise budget. If your interactive is competing with your batch within the same budget, that’s the part we can fix by splitting.

13:19 Jules Bennett: So two projects, two keys, separate limits.

13:22 Liam O'Rourke: Yes. We can set batch project as best-effort and interactive as enterprise protected. That way under pressure batch gets throttled first.

13:33 Anika Rao: That seems like the right architecture.

13:36 Sana Qureshi: Any security implications with multiple keys.

13:39 Liam O'Rourke: No, it’s still within your enterprise workspace. Same audit logs, same controls. You just have separate credentials. You’ll want to store them in your secret manager.

13:49 Martin Schulte: Okay.

13:51 Rachel Kim: Let’s do a quick metrics review, then we can close with next steps. Rafael, can you give us the “before vs after” in one minute.

14:00 Rafael Mendes: Before enabling protection: under fleet pressure, your chat requests were getting queued behind other traffic, queue depth spiked, p99 went into double digits, and then you saw some 5xx due to upstream timeouts.

14:13 Rafael Mendes: After enabling: queue depth is bounded, p99 mostly under 5 seconds, 5xx rate down materially. We see 429 admission control during your overlap window. Those 429s are fast and protect the rest.

14:27 Anika Rao: Great.

14:29 Martin Schulte: Our numbers: p99 from ~15–18 sec down to ~4–6 sec. 5xx almost gone. 429 from basically 0.2% to 4–6% during peak.

14:42 Rachel Kim: Perfect. So we need to bring that 429 peak down for interactive. That’s the key follow-up.

14:50 Jules Bennett: We’ll split batch and interactive this sprint. But we also want the temporary burst increase while we do that.

14:58 Liam O'Rourke: That’s fair. We can target approving by end of week. We’ll need your proposed concurrency numbers.

15:07 Anika Rao: We can send. What do you need, exactly.

15:10 Rafael Mendes: For interactive: average and peak RPS, and concurrent streams if you stream. For batch: same plus the job schedule.

15:20 Martin Schulte: Okay.

15:22 Sana Qureshi: And we’ll want a note on how this aligns with the SLO we have.

15:27 Rachel Kim: We’ll include that. The intent is to preserve the SLO for the protected enterprise route. The burst exception is within that framework, not outside it.

15:38 Owen Phillips: Also, please make sure your engineers stop parsing the human-readable error message. Use the headers. I’m saying this because I’ve seen clients key off “Too Many Requests” text and it changes.

15:49 Jules Bennett: Yeah, guilty. We’ll fix.

15:52 Rachel Kim: One more question: you mentioned Azure OpenAI and Anthropic in the escalation email—are you actively comparing behavior?

16:00 Anika Rao: We are, yes. Mainly on stability. We don’t love being tied to one provider. But honestly, your improvements this week helped.

16:10 Rachel Kim: Understood. Our goal is to make the behavior predictable and supportable. That’s what this protection work is for.

16:17 Liam O'Rourke: And if you do want to evaluate dedicated later, we can do it in a controlled pilot, but no pressure.

16:24 Anika Rao: Okay.

16:26 Martin Schulte: One question: can you expose these 429 reason code counts in your console? Right now we scrape headers.

16:33 Liam O'Rourke: We have internal views and we’re rolling out customer-facing transparency in phases. Short term, we can provide a dashboard export or weekly report.

16:45 Rachel Kim: For now, we’ll share screenshots and the mapping. Longer term, yes, it’ll be in the console.

16:53 Sana Qureshi: We prefer written weekly until it’s in the console.

16:56 Rachel Kim: Got it.

17:00 Rachel Kim: Okay, last five minutes—let’s align on the exception handling so Sana is comfortable.

17:06 Sana Qureshi: I just want to ensure changes are controlled. We need: who approves, what monitoring, and how we rollback.

17:14 Rachel Kim: Approval: Liam (TAM) + Rafael (SRE) + me for customer impact. Monitoring: shed rate, latency SLO burn, and 5xx. Rollback: if shed rate exceeds threshold for sustained window or if enterprise SLO starts burning faster than acceptable.

17:31 Rafael Mendes: And the change itself is feature-flagged and region-specific. So we can roll back in eu-west without touching us-east.

17:39 Martin Schulte: That’s good.

17:41 Jules Bennett: Can we get an SLA-style statement that batch may be throttled first.

17:46 Rachel Kim: We can provide language that best-effort workloads may receive 429 under pressure to preserve protected route behavior. We won’t frame it as “we guarantee batch,” but we’ll give recommended patterns so batch completes via backoff.

18:03 Anika Rao: That’s acceptable.

18:05 Liam O'Rourke: Cool. Then the immediate steps are: you send retry policy + concurrency numbers, we send the reason code one-pager + dashboard screenshots, and we evaluate the +20% burst exception.

18:20 Rachel Kim: Exactly.

18:22 Martin Schulte: Can we also schedule the technical session? Jules can join.

18:26 Liam O'Rourke: Yep. I’ll send a calendar invite for early next week.

18:31 Rachel Kim: Anything else before we wrap?

18:34 Anika Rao: No, this is good. Thanks for the transparency.

18:37 Sana Qureshi: Thanks.

18:38 Rachel Kim: Thanks everyone. We’ll send the recap by tomorrow.

(End of transcript)
